newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Lithuania 2nd round elections attract few voters.
newsitem.headline: Lithuania 2nd round elections attract few voters.

text.p: Polling stations across Lithuania reported a low turn-out on Sunday for the second round of a parliamentary election likely to seal the return of independence hero Vytautas Landsbergis to govern the Baltic nation.
The parliament press centre reported a 24.44 percent turn-out seven hours after voting started compared with 30.49 percent at the same time during the first round of the election on October 20.
Last month a total of only 55 percent of eligible voters cast votes compared with around 75 percent in the 1992 election, a year after Lithuania declared independence from the Soviet Union.

Four years ago the government led by Landsbergis was replaced by the former communists, renamed the Lithuanian Democratic Labour Party (LDLP), but diplomatic sources were confident that Landsbergis and his Homeland Union will regain control this year.
Analysts say Lithuanian voters, many of whom are struggling on a daily basis to make ends meet, are fed up with politics and prefer to spend their Sunday away from the polling stations.
Polling stations opened at 0500 GMT (0700 local time) and are scheduled to close at 1900 GMT but the final result may not be known for several days.
The second round of the election works on a majority vote system with the 65 seats up for grabs to be won by candidates with the highest number of votes. A total of 130 are standing.
The first round of the election held last month allocated blocks in the house to political parties.
Twenty-four parties ran but only five got past the five percent threshhold required to gain entry into the 141-seat parliament.

The Homeland Union took 33 of the 70 seats in that round while its furture coalition partner, the Christian Democrats, won 11 seats. The LDLP took 10, the Centre Union nine and the Social Democrats seven.
The Homeland Union also secured two seats under the majority-vote single-mandate system being held today.
The results from four distrcist were declared invalid because less than 40 percent of eligible voters cast ballots and will be held again next spring.
